title: Naxalbari Uprising and Left Radicalization in Bengal
subtitle: A peasant movement in North Bengal became a rallying point for a wider revolutionary communist current.
summary: In February–May 1967, sharecroppers and poor peasants in the Naxalbari area of Darjeeling district protested land relations, with support from local CPI(M) organizers, according to historian Vanessa Corrado. Corrado dates a police firing at Bengai Jote to 25 May 1967 and recounts the preceding confrontation partly through former activist Sanjay Mitra’s oral testimony. The movement also prompted organizing in Calcutta: a solidarity committee appeared in July–August 1967, followed by an all-India coordination committee in November. By 1969, revolutionary circles around Charu Mazumdar supported forming the CPI(ML); Ritanjan Das independently places its formation announcement in May that year. Corrado describes the movement’s urban base as including students and workers, while stressing that revolutionary groups were not unified.
heroTagline: From peasant protest in Darjeeling district to radical organizing in Calcutta.
whyItMatters: The episode linked rural land protest to urban political mobilization and an organizational break within the communist movement. Corrado’s account shows how Naxalbari became a rallying point, while also warning that later narratives can flatten a socially diverse and internally divided movement. Details of the firing and its immediate causes remain sensitive and should be read with attribution: part of Corrado’s narrative relies on a former participant’s oral account.
historicalDebate: Corrado describes the 25 May police firing and reports deaths, but her text’s opening narrative relies in part on former activist Sanjay Mitra’s oral testimony and contains an explicit correction of casualty counts within that testimony. This chapter omits casualty numbers and does not treat responsibility for the events preceding the firing as settled. Das’s brief overview describes the movement and subsequent party formation but does not independently resolve the sequence at Bengai Jote.
contentWarnings: This chapter discusses political violence and police firing.
